talk: A VC fund backs many startups knowing most will fail. A handful of huge winners pay for everything, which is called the power law. That's why investors ask whether a company could be enormous, not just whether it will work.

terms.meaning: A few outcomes are far bigger than all the rest combined.
One investment that pays back the whole fund on its own.
What came back divided by what went in.

questions.prompt: A $100M fund invests $5M each in 20 startups. 14 fail completely, 5 return just their money, and 1 returns $250M. What does the fund get back in total?
questions.hint: Add the survivors to the big winner.
working: 5 x $5M = $25M from the five that returned their money.
whyNot: $250M is the one big winner. The 5 that returned their money add $25M.
$250M + $5M = $255M counts just one of the five.
$250M + 10 x $5M = $300M counts 10 survivors. Only 5 returned their money.

questions.prompt: What's the fund's money multiple: total back divided by the $100M in?
questions.hint: Everything back divided by everything in.
whyNot: $300M / $100M = 3 would need $300M back. The fund got $275M.
($275M - $100M) / $100M = 1.75 is the gain on top. The money multiple counts everything that came back.

questions.prompt: Without the one big winner, how much would the fund get back?
working: Only the 5 that returned their money: 5 x $5M = $25M.
$25M back on $100M in. The one big winner is the whole game.
whyNot: The 5 that returned their money still count: 5 x $5M = $25M.
$100M - $25M = $75M is what the fund would lose, not what it gets back.
Breaking even needs a big winner. Without it, only $25M comes back.

penalty.prompt: A {fund} fund gets back {each} from each of {n} survivors and {big} from one big winner. Everything else fails. What's the money multiple?
penalty.hint: Everything back divided by everything in.
working: {n * each + big|usd} / {fund} = {(n * each + big) / fund|num} times.

traps.why: That counts only the big winner. Add the survivors.
That's the gain on top. The money multiple counts everything that came back.

call.title: Matching the investor
call.prompt: A big fund will put in $5M for 20%, but only if your plan could make the club worth $200M, enough to return their whole fund. Your honest plan gets to about $40M. A smaller fund that's happy with a $40M outcome offers $2M for 15%, enough for about 1,000 more fans a match. The big money would add about 1,500.

options.label: Pitch the $200M dream to the big fund
options.result: Overpromising wins the money, but a $200M target becomes your boss.

later.text: The big targets are missed. The investor forces costly changes: $10,000 a matchday in new staff.

options.label: Take $2M from the smaller fund
options.result: Good call. Match the investor to the plan. A $40M outcome is a great result for a fund that expects one, and 1,000 x $18 = $18,000 a matchday.

options.label: Raise from neither
options.result: The smaller raise would have added 1,000 x $18 = $18,000 a matchday.

takeaway: VC funds need a few giant wins. Pick investors whose maths fits your plan.
